Swan Lake. One of the most famous and frequently performed classical ballets in history, Swan Lake is a canonical four-act ballet composed by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, his first score written specifically for the ballet medium. The story centers on Prince Siegfried, who is pressured to choose a bride for his birthday. He escapes to hunt swans in the forest and encounters Odette, the Swan Queen, cursed by the evil sorcerer Von Rothbart to turn into a swan by day and can only take human form at night near a lake created by her mother's tears. Siegfried falls deeply in love with her. However, Von Rothbart's daughter Odile, the black swan, disguises herself as Odette to trick Siegfried into breaking his vow of fidelity. The ballet ends tragically in most versions, with Siegfried and Odette drowning themselves in the lake, breaking Von Rothbart's spell and uniting in the afterlife. The dual role of Odette and Odile is famously demanding, traditionally requiring the ballerina to perform thirty-two consecutive fouettés in Act III. The ballet premiered in 1877 at Moscow's Bolshoi Theatre to initial failure, but a subsequent revival at the Mariinsky Theatre in Saint Petersburg in 1895, choreographed by Marius Petipa for Acts One and Three and Lev Ivanov for Acts Two and Four, established it as a masterpiece. That 1895 revival became the definitive version and remains so today. Act Two features the famous Dance of the Little Swans, a ensemble piece for four dancers holding hands and moving in perfect unison. Swan Lake also introduced the convention of the white act, where the female corps de ballet is dressed in white tutus symbolizing purity and tragedy. The ballet remains a cornerstone of classical dance technique and romantic musical theater, celebrated for its demanding choreography and evocative, emotionally complex score.
